name: Nehemiah
bio:
Nehemiah son of Hachaliah served as cupbearer to King Artaxerxes of Persia at the palace in Susa. In the twentieth year of the king's reign, his brother Hanani and other men arrived from Judah and told him that the Jewish remnant there lived in great trouble and disgrace, with Jerusalem's wall broken down and its gates burned. Nehemiah wept, mourned, and fasted for days, praying to the LORD and confessing Israel's sins, and asking God to grant him success and favor before the king as he prepared to make a request of him (Nehemiah 1:1-11). His own leadership in rebuilding Jerusalem's wall is told in detail in the chapters ahead.  When King Artaxerxes noticed Nehemiah's sorrow, Nehemiah explained his grief over Jerusalem's ruin and, after praying silently, asked to be sent there to rebuild it; the king granted his request, set him a timeframe, and gave him letters of safe passage and a supply of timber, along with an armed escort. Sanballat the Horonite and Tobiah the Ammonite official were furious to hear a man had come seeking Israel's welfare. After three days in Jerusalem, Nehemiah secretly surveyed the broken walls and burned gates by night before telling anyone his plan. He then rallied the Jews, priests, and nobles to rebuild the wall, telling them of God's favor and the king's support; they agreed at once. When Sanballat, Tobiah, and Geshem the Arab mocked them as rebels against the king, Nehemiah answered that God would give them success and that these men had no share, right, or claim in Jerusalem (Nehemiah 2:1-20).

 When Sanballat mocked the Jews' efforts before the Samarian army and Tobiah scoffed that a fox could knock down their wall, Nehemiah prayed for God to turn their contempt back on them, and the work continued until the wall was half built. As Sanballat, Tobiah, and the Arabs, Ammonites, and Ashdodites heard of this progress, they conspired to attack Jerusalem and stop the work; Nehemiah prayed and posted an armed watch. When the people grew discouraged and the enemies planned a surprise attack, Nehemiah stationed families with swords, spears, and bows at the vulnerable points and rallied the nobles and people not to be afraid but to fight for their families and homes. From then on, half the workers built while the other half stood guard in armor, every builder working with a weapon at his side; Nehemiah kept a trumpeter ready to summon everyone to wherever an attack came, and had the workers lodge inside Jerusalem at night to serve as guards, with no one changing out of their clothes except to wash (Nehemiah 4:1-23).

 Amid the building effort, the poor cried out that debt, famine, and royal taxes had forced them to mortgage their land and sell their own children into slavery to fellow Jews. Angered, Nehemiah confronted the nobles and officials who were charging interest on their own people, called a great assembly, and shamed them into agreeing to return the mortgaged fields, vineyards, and houses and stop collecting interest; he made the priests swear to it and shook out the fold of his garment as a sign of the ruin awaiting anyone who broke the promise, and the people kept their word. Nehemiah also noted that during his twelve years as governor, unlike his predecessors, he and his associates had never taken the governor's food allowance or exacted the usual taxes from the people, despite feeding over a hundred and fifty people daily at his own table, because he feared God and felt the people's burden too heavy already; he asked God to remember him favorably for all he had done for them (Nehemiah 5:1-19).

 When the wall neared completion, Sanballat and Geshem tried four times to lure Nehemiah away to a village on the plain of Ono, intending to harm him; he refused each time, saying he could not abandon the work. Sanballat then sent an open letter accusing Nehemiah of planning to rebel and crown himself king, hoping the threat of exposure would frighten him into stopping; Nehemiah denied the charge as pure invention and prayed for strength. Shemaiah son of Delaiah, hired by Tobiah and Sanballat, then urged Nehemiah to hide in the temple from assassins, but Nehemiah recognized the trap and refused to flee or sin out of fear; he asked God to remember Tobiah, Sanballat, and the prophetess Noadiah and the other hired prophets for their schemes. Despite all this, the wall was finished in fifty-two days, and even Judah's enemies were humbled, recognizing God's hand in the work — though Tobiah, tied to many of Judah's nobles by marriage, kept sending letters to unsettle Nehemiah even afterward (Nehemiah 6:1-19).

 Once the wall was finished and the doors set up, Nehemiah appointed his brother Hanani and Hananiah, ruler of the citadel, over Jerusalem's security, since Hananiah was faithful and feared God more than most; he had them keep the gates shut until well into the morning and organize the thinly populated city's residents into watches. Nehemiah then gathered the nobles, officials, and people to be registered by genealogy, and found the old record of those who had first returned under Zerubbabel (Nehemiah 7:1-73).

 When the people heard Ezra read the Law and wept, Nehemiah joined Ezra and the Levites in declaring the day holy and joyful rather than sorrowful, urging them to feast and share with those in need; the people obeyed and kept a joyous Feast of Tabernacles unmatched since the days of Joshua son of Nun (Nehemiah 8:9-17).

 Nehemiah sealed this covenant first, followed by the priests, Levites, and chiefs of the people; its signers bound themselves and their families to follow God's law, not to intermarry with the surrounding peoples, to honor the sabbath and the sabbath year by not trading on holy days and releasing debts every seventh year, to pay an annual temple tax, to supply wood for the altar by lot, and to bring the firstfruits, firstborn, and tithes to the temple so that it would never be neglected (Nehemiah 10:1-39).

 At the wall's dedication, Nehemiah brought the Levites and singers from the surrounding villages to Jerusalem for a joyful ceremony of thanksgiving. The priests and Levites purified themselves, the people, the gates, and the wall; Nehemiah then led the princes of Judah up onto the wall in two great processions giving thanks in opposite directions, meeting at the temple, where they offered great sacrifices amid such rejoicing that it could be heard far away (Nehemiah 12:27-43).

 Returning to Jerusalem after time away in Babylon with King Artaxerxes, Nehemiah discovered that Eliashib the priest had allied with Tobiah and given him a temple storeroom; he threw out Tobiah's belongings, had the room purified, and restored it to its proper use. Finding that the Levites' portions had gone undelivered and they had abandoned their temple duties for their fields, he confronted the officials, reassembled the Levites, and appointed trustworthy treasurers — Shelemiah, Zadok, Pedaiah, and Hanan — to distribute supplies fairly. He also found people treading wine presses, selling produce, and trading with Tyrian merchants on the sabbath; he rebuked Judah's nobles for profaning the holy day as their ancestors had, and had Jerusalem's gates shut from before the sabbath until it ended, posting his own servants and purified Levites to guard them and turning away merchants who tried to camp outside the walls. Finally, he found Jews who had married foreign wives whose children could no longer speak Hebrew; he rebuked them harshly, invoking Solomon's downfall through foreign wives as a warning, and drove away a priest who had married into Sanballat's family for defiling the priesthood. Nehemiah closed his memoir by asking God to remember him favorably for all he had done to restore proper worship and purity to Jerusalem (Nehemiah 13:1-31).
